tagline.text: A gentle city where sea breezes meet college-town romance

children.text: The capital of Negros Oriental, known as the "City of Gentle People." It is a quiet college town home to Silliman University and a gateway to Apo Island, Dauin diving, and Siquijor, with low prices and good safety that make it popular with long-term visitors too.

Dumaguete is the capital of Negros Oriental Province, sitting at the southeastern tip of Negros Island and facing Cebu Island across the Tañon Strait. With a population of only around 130,000, it is a small city, yet among Filipinos it is famous by the nickname "City of Gentle People." Car horns are rarely heard, tricycle drivers are comparatively honest, and the mood stays calm even when strolling the seaside boulevard late at night.
What shaped the city's character is Silliman University, founded by American Presbyterian missionaries in

. One of the oldest American-founded private universities in Asia, it occupies the heart of the city with its spacious campus, acacia-lined avenues, and old wooden buildings. The large student population means cafes, bookstores, and inexpensive restaurants are everywhere, and the university's tradition of marine biology research even helped give rise to the nearby Apo Island marine sanctuary.

The city's own sights are modest — the seaside promenade Rizal Boulevard, the Dumaguete belfry that began as an 18th-century watchtower against pirate raids, and St. Catherine's Cathedral. Dumaguete's real value, though, lies in being a "base." A
30-minute
drive reaches Dauin, a world-class muck-diving spot; a
1-hour
drive reaches Malatapay, the jump-off port for Apo Island, the twin volcanic Twin Lakes, and Casaroro Falls; and a
1-hour
boat ride reaches Siquijor Island.

Prices are clearly lower than in Manila or Cebu, and hospitals, large supermarkets, and banks are all available, so many Korean retirees, language-study students, and long-term diver residents settle here. The city suits travelers who want relaxed city living paired with nearby nature rather than a flashy resort, and those hoping to combine a loop through Negros, Siquijor, and Apo Island.
A seaside promenade running about

, lined with old street lamps and benches beneath acacia trees. Around sunset, locals come out to jog and stroll, and the street across from it is packed with bars and restaurants, making it a good spot for dinner too.
State your purpose at the main gate and you can usually walk the campus freely. Silliman Hall, a wooden building from the early
, the anthropology museum, and the seaside campus views are impressive. On weekdays during term time, the student food strip is lively too.

The stone belfry standing in the square beside the cathedral is a city symbol that began as a watchtower against Moro pirate raids. In front of it you can see locals lighting candles and praying, and it photographs beautifully once the night lights come on.
Dumaguete is famous nationwide for silvanas, a cashew-meringue-and-buttercream pastry, and the Sans Rival cake. Sans Rival Cakes and Pastries, which opened in
, is a stop nearly every traveler makes, and many buy frozen silvanas to take home as gifts.
The Dauin coast, about
15km

south of the city center, is a renowned spot for "muck diving" — spotting small creatures like seahorses, frogfish, and cuttlefish. Beach diving is inexpensive, and many dive shops offer beginner courses.
Apo Island, famous for snorkeling alongside sea turtles, is Dumaguete's most popular day-trip destination. Hotels and dive shops offer tours that include pickup, bangka transfer, and lunch.
In the mountains behind the city, at an elevation of about
, lie the twin lakes of Balinsasayao and Danao and Casaroro Falls in Valencia. In half a day you can enjoy cool forest scenery completely unlike the coast.

Every Wednesday, a traditional livestock market for buying and selling cattle, pigs, and goats is held at Malatapay in Zamboanguita to the south. The food stalls that carve and sell whole roasted lechon pig on the spot are especially famous, and since it's the same place the Apo Island boats depart from, it pairs well with that trip.

Tricycles are the main means of transport downtown, with very cheap base fares, and the Silliman–Rizal Boulevard–belfry stretch is easily walkable. For Dauin or Malatapay, take a southbound jeepney or bus; for mountain destinations like Twin Lakes, a day-long chartered vehicle (about
) or chartered tricycle is more convenient.
Dumaguete is shielded by the Negros mountain range, so it sees comparatively little typhoon damage even by Philippine standards. From
December
to
May
is the dry season, when the sea is calm and visibility is good — the best time for diving and Apo Island trips. March to
May
is the hottest but the skies are clear, while December to
February
brings cool breezes good for city strolls.
From
June
to
November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and from July to
October
, typhoons can cancel boats to Siquijor and Cebu on some days. Still, all-day rain is uncommon, so city sightseeing is generally fine. In late
November
, the Sandurot Festival celebrating the city's founding is held, and from April to
May
, downtown gets busy with Silliman University's graduation season.

For a first visit, staying around Rizal Boulevard and near Silliman University in the city center is most convenient. You can walk to restaurants, cafes, and money changers, and there are many clean business hotels in the
range per night. If diving is your goal, dive resorts on the Dauin coast to the south (about
per night, many with diving packages included) greatly cut down travel time. Long-term residents often use monthly-rental condos or apartelles on the edge of town.

True to its college-town character, food here is cheap and varied. At the end of the seaside promenade, food stalls set up every evening selling fried skewers called tempura (a kind of fried fish cake) and grilled squid, and around the market there are many carinderias where you pick rice and viands. Budbud kabog, a millet rice cake, and thick hot chocolate tsokolate are a favorite local Dumaguete-style breakfast. Popular souvenirs include silvanas from Sans Rival and dried fish and cashews from the market. The boulevard also has many Western-style restaurants and bars where retirees and divers spend their evenings.
Downtown has plenty of bank ATMs, but many small resorts on Apo Island and in Dauin, and restaurants by the mountain lakes, only accept cash, so bring plenty of small bills.
Agree on the tricycle fare before boarding at the airport or the port. For short downtown rides, about
per person is the going rate.
Apo Island tours need to be booked by the day before to secure your preferred date, and they can be canceled on the morning of if the sea is rough, so avoid scheduling it for your last day.
Sans Rival silvanas are kept frozen, so if your travel time is long, ask for them to be packed in an insulated bag.
Splitting your base by purpose — Dauin for diving, Apo Island for turtle snorkeling, Siquijor for a quiet retreat — makes for an efficient route.
Twin Lakes sits at high elevation where fog and rain are frequent in the afternoon, so it's best to go up in the morning.
For sunset photos along Rizal Boulevard, the sun actually sets behind the mountains, so the best time is the
20 minutes
around dusk when the sky over the sea turns pink.
If combining this with the whale shark tour at Oslob in southern Cebu, taking the early-morning Liloan–Sibulan boat lets you make the round trip in a single day.
Safety is generally good, but avoid walking alone late at night along quiet stretches of the coast or in market back alleys, and keep your belongings in front of your body.
In the marine protected areas of Dauin and Apo Island, stepping on coral or touching turtles is prohibited, and fines are imposed if caught.
During the rainy and typhoon season, boats to Siquijor and Cebu can be canceled without notice, so don't schedule island trips for the day before your return flight.
Dengue-carrying mosquitoes are present, so be sure to use mosquito repellent, especially during the rainy season.
There have been scams involving real estate or business offers aimed at long-term residents, so verify through the local expat community or a licensed agent.
